questions.q: In BC, who holds absolute title to all land?
choices: The registered fee simple owner
The Crown
The local municipality
The Land Title and Survey Authority
questions.explain: Only the Crown holds absolute title. Private owners hold estates granted out of the Crown's title; the largest of these is the fee simple.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Who really owns land in BC

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the limits on a fee simple owner's rights?
choices: The Crown's power of expropriation and tax sale
Land use and building regulations
Other people's common law rights
The right of the previous owner to buy the land back
questions.explain: A fee simple is limited only by expropriation and tax sale, land use and building regulation, and other people's common law rights. A previous owner has no general buy-back right.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Who really owns land in BC

questions.q: Who owns Indian Act reserve land?
choices: The First Nation, in fee simple
The provincial Crown
The federal government, with the First Nation holding a collective right to use and occupy it
Individual band members
questions.explain: Reserve land is owned by the federal government. The First Nation has a collective right to use and occupy the land set aside for it.

questions.q: Aboriginal title can be transferred to whom?
choices: Anyone, like a fee simple
Only to other members of the same First Nation
Only to the Crown
Only to a corporation owned by the First Nation
questions.explain: Aboriginal title is held collectively for present and future generations and can be alienated only to the Crown. That's one reason it isn't an estate in the ordinary sense.

questions.q: A new waste-transfer station opens next to a residential street and nearby house values fall. Which characteristic of real property does this illustrate?
choices: Durability
Immobility (externalities)
Divisibility of ownership
Indivisibility of services
questions.explain: Because land can't be moved, it's exposed to whatever happens next door. Effects from outside the property's boundaries are called externalities, a consequence of immobility.

questions.q: Why is the claim "they're not making any more land" misleading for urban markets?
choices: The physical surface of the earth is growing
The supply of usable urban land grows through farm conversion, rezoning, intensification and better transport
Land values never rise
Zoning has no effect on supply
questions.explain: The physical surface is fixed, but the supply of usable urban land is not: farmland converts, zoning changes allow more density, sites intensify, and transport makes distant land usable.

questions.q: A sound 1970s office building is demolished to build a 30-storey tower. Which concept explains this?
choices: Its physical life ended
Its economic life ended before its physical life
Escheat
Permissive waste
questions.explain: A building's economic life ends when the site is worth more redeveloped. That usually happens long before the building physically wears out.

questions.q: In a mortgage, who is the mortgagor?
choices: The lender
The borrower who grants the mortgage
The mortgage broker
The mortgage insurer
questions.explain: The mortgagor is the borrower, who gives (grants) the mortgage to the lender as security. The lender is the mortgagee.

questions.q: A buyer borrows 85% of the purchase price from a federally regulated bank. What is required, and whom does it protect?
choices: Title insurance, protecting the buyer
Mortgage default insurance, protecting the lender
Life insurance, protecting the buyer's family
Nothing; only loans above 95% need insurance
questions.explain: Loans above 80% of value are high-ratio loans. The borrower must buy mortgage default insurance (CMHC, Sagen or Canada Guaranty), which protects the lender if the borrower defaults.

questions.q: A seller wants to list at their BC Assessment value because "that's what the government says it's worth." What's the best response?
choices: Agree; assessed value is market value
Explain that assessed value is a mass-valuation figure from a fixed date and isn't the same as market value
List at double the assessed value
Refuse the listing
questions.explain: BC Assessment sets values for taxation using mass appraisal at a fixed date. It's useful context, but assessed value is not market value.

questions.q: Which is typical of the IC&I market compared with residential?
choices: More transactions per year, mostly on standard forms
Fewer, larger, more analytical deals with custom lawyer-drafted contracts
Decisions made emotionally by the occupants
Almost all properties marketed on MLS®
questions.explain: IC&I deals are fewer and larger, decided analytically (often by several people or a board), financed in complex ways and documented with long custom contracts.

questions.q: Under the Law and Equity Act, English law as of what date applies in BC unless changed or locally inapplicable?
choices: 1 July 1867
19 November 1858
20 July 1871
14 October 1066
questions.explain: English law as it stood on 19 November 1858 applies in BC, which is why medieval concepts like the doctrine of estates still govern BC land.

questions.q: A landowner dies with no will and no heirs. What happens to the land?
choices: It goes to the nearest neighbour
It escheats to the Crown
It's sold and the money goes to charity
The municipality takes it for back taxes
questions.explain: Escheat: when an owner dies without a will and without heirs, the land goes to the Crown.

questions.q: "To my sister Meera for life, then to my nephew Dev." What is Dev?
choices: The reversioner
The remainderman
The life tenant
A joint tenant
questions.explain: Dev receives the fee simple after Meera's life estate ends, so he's the remainderman. If the property went back to the grantor instead, the grantor would be the reversioner.

questions.q: A life tenant sells her life estate to a buyer. When does the buyer's estate end?
choices: On the buyer's death
On the original life tenant's death
After 99 years
When the remainderman decides
questions.explain: The buyer holds an estate pur autre vie, measured by the life of the original life tenant. It ends when she dies, not when the buyer dies.

questions.q: A property subject to a life estate has a mortgage. Who pays the mortgage principal?
choices: The life tenant
The remainderman (or reversioner)
They split it equally
The lender writes it off
questions.explain: The life tenant pays running costs, taxes and mortgage interest. The remainderman or reversioner pays the principal and insurance premiums.

questions.q: A life tenant lets the roof deteriorate and does nothing about it. What kind of waste is this, and is the life tenant generally liable?
choices: Voluntary waste; liable
Permissive waste; generally not liable
Ameliorating waste; liable but no damages
Equitable waste; liable
questions.explain: Allowing property to deteriorate through inaction is permissive waste. A life tenant is generally not liable for it.

questions.q: A life estate is granted "without impeachment for waste." The life tenant deliberately burns the house down. Is the life tenant liable?
choices: No; the phrase excuses all waste
Yes; the phrase excuses only the three common law types, not equitable waste
Only if the house was insured
Only if the remainderman lives on the property
questions.explain: "Without impeachment for waste" excuses voluntary, permissive and ameliorating waste. Equitable (malicious) waste is excused only if the document says so expressly.

questions.q: A buyer completes a purchase. A tenant is in occupation under an unregistered 2-year lease. Is the buyer bound by the lease?
choices: No; unregistered interests never bind a buyer
Yes; leases of 3 years or less with actual occupation bind a buyer even if unregistered
Only if the buyer was told about it in writing
Only for residential tenancies
questions.explain: Land Title Act s.23 makes a lease of 3 years or less, with actual occupation, binding on a buyer even though it isn't registered. Always investigate who's in possession.

questions.q: Lot A has a registered right of way over a driveway on Lot B. Which is the servient tenement?
choices: Lot A
Lot B
Both
Neither; it's an easement in gross
questions.explain: The servient tenement carries the burden (Lot B, which must allow passage). The dominant tenement benefits (Lot A).
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: A neighbour has used a path across your seller's land openly for 30 years. In BC, has an easement been created by prescription?
choices: Yes, after 20 years of use
Yes, after 30 years of use
No; prescriptive easements have been abolished in BC
Only if the neighbour paid property taxes
questions.explain: Easements by prescription (long use) are abolished in BC. Easements arise by statute, express grant or, in limited cases, implication.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: BC Hydro holds a right of way for a power line across a farm, but owns no neighbouring land. What allows this?
choices: A profit à prendre
A statutory right of way under Land Title Act s.218, which doesn't need a dominant tenement
A licence
A building scheme
questions.explain: Ordinary easements need a dominant tenement. A statutory right of way under LTA s.218 is the exception, used by utilities, governments and others.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: Which is NOT a requirement for a restrictive covenant to run with the land?
choices: It must be negative in substance
It must benefit the covenantee's land
It must be signed by every owner in the neighbourhood
The person bound must have notice (registration is notice)
questions.explain: The requirements are: negative; benefits the covenantee's land; both lands precisely identified; intended to bind the land; notice. There's no need for every neighbour to sign.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: What did the Supreme Court of Canada decide in Crystal Square (2020)?
choices: Positive covenants always run with the land
Positive covenants never bind later owners in any circumstances
Positive covenants generally don't run with the land, but a later owner who voluntarily paid for years was bound by a new contract formed through conduct
Restrictive covenants must be renewed every 20 years
questions.explain: The court confirmed the general rule that positive covenants don't run with the land, but found the strata had become bound by its conduct of paying maintenance fees for years in exchange for parking.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: A developer wants identical design restrictions on every lot in a new subdivision. What does the developer register?
choices: A statutory right of way
A Declaration of Creation of Building Scheme under LTA s.220
A profit à prendre
A caveat
questions.explain: A building scheme imposes a common set of restrictive covenants on lots sold by a common vendor. It's created by registering a declaration under LTA s.220(1).
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: Which statement about a profit à prendre is correct?
choices: It must be attached to a dominant tenement
It can be held in gross and can't be implied
It must be for a fixed term
It's the same as a licence
questions.explain: A profit à prendre (a right to take minerals, timber, fish and so on) can exist in gross, doesn't need a fixed term, and can't be created by implication.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: An old covenant limits a lot to single-family use in an area since rezoned for high-rise towers. Which provision lets a court cancel or modify it?
choices: Land Title Act s.23
Property Law Act s.35
Partition of Property Act s.6
Occupiers Liability Act s.3
questions.explain: PLA s.35 lets the BC Supreme Court cancel or modify easements, SRWs, building schemes and restrictive covenants that are obsolete, block reasonable use without benefit, or that the beneficiary has agreed to release.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: Which statement about a licence is correct?
choices: It's an interest in land that runs with the land
It's a personal contractual permission; it can't be registered and doesn't bind a buyer
It's a registered easement for a fixed term
It's created automatically after 10 years of use
questions.explain: A licence is personal permission to do something on another's land. It isn't an interest in land, can't be registered and doesn't run with the land.
questions.ref: Lesson 2 · Interests less than an estate

questions.q: How far into the airspace does a BC landowner's ownership extend today?
choices: To the heavens
100 metres
As far as the owner can make effective use of it
Only to the height of existing buildings
questions.explain: The old "to the heavens" rule has been modified: an owner owns the airspace only to the extent they can effectively use it, and federal law lets aircraft pass overhead.

questions.q: Which is true about water licences in BC?
choices: They're registered on title in the land title office
They're held by the province and can be cancelled after 3 consecutive years of non-use or non-payment
A household well always needs a licence
Unpaid fees are wiped out on a sale
questions.explain: Under the Water Sustainability Act, water belongs to the province. Licences aren't in the land title office, can be cancelled after 3 consecutive years of non-use or non-payment, and pass to a buyer with any arrears. Domestic groundwater use is the main exception.

questions.q: A neighbour excavates to the lot line and both the soil and the house next door slump. What does the natural right of support cover?
choices: Both the land and the house
The land only; the building needs an easement of support
The house only
Nothing; there's no right of support in BC
questions.explain: Every parcel has a natural right to vertical and lateral support for the land itself. Buildings don't have that natural right; it requires an easement of support.

questions.q: Under the Stack v. T. Eaton test, an item attached to a building, even slightly, is presumed to be what?
choices: A chattel
A fixture
A licence
Neither; it depends only on the price
questions.explain: Items attached even slightly are presumed fixtures; items resting by their own weight are presumed chattels. Either presumption can be rebutted by the degree and object of the attachment.

questions.q: A cattle-handling machine is welded to a bracket only so it won't move while in use. How did a BC court treat a similar item?
choices: As a fixture, because it was welded
As a chattel, because it was attached for the better use of the machine, not to improve the land
As part of the building scheme
As an easement
questions.explain: In Monical (2013 BCSC), the attachment was only to stabilize the machine while in use, which rebutted the fixture presumption. It remained a chattel.

questions.q: What are the four unities required for a joint tenancy?
choices: Time, title, interest, possession
Time, title, income, price
Title, tax, interest, possession
Time, transfer, intention, purchase
questions.explain: Joint tenants must take at the same time, under the same document, with identical interests, and each must be entitled to possession of the whole.

questions.q: A will leaves a building "equally to my daughters, Ana and Bea." How do they hold it?
choices: As joint tenants, because all four unities exist
As tenants in common, because BC law presumes tenancy in common unless joint tenancy is clearly stated
As life tenants
As remaindermen
questions.explain: Under the Property Law Act, co-owners are presumed to be tenants in common unless the document clearly creates a joint tenancy.

questions.q: Two joint tenants own a duplex. One dies with a will leaving everything to his son. Who gets his interest?
choices: The son, under the will
The surviving joint tenant, by right of survivorship
It's split between the son and the survivor
The Crown
questions.explain: The right of survivorship means a joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s). It can't be left by will.

questions.q: X, Y and Z are joint tenants. X sells her interest to Q. What's the result?
choices: Y, Z and Q are all joint tenants
Y and Z remain joint tenants between themselves of two-thirds, and are tenants in common with Q
The sale is void without Y and Z's consent
The whole joint tenancy becomes a life estate
questions.explain: The sale severs the joint tenancy as to X's share only. Q holds one-third as a tenant in common; Y and Z remain joint tenants of the other two-thirds.

questions.q: Two tenants in common each own 50% of a property and can't agree on selling. What can either of them do?
choices: Nothing; both must agree
Apply under the Partition of Property Act, and the court must order a sale unless there's good reason not to
Register a building scheme
Evict the other
questions.explain: Under Partition of Property Act s.6, a co-owner holding at least half the interest can obtain a court-ordered sale unless there's good reason to refuse (ter Borg v. Morris, 2012).

questions.q: A trespasser refuses to leave a property. What must the occupier do before using self-help?
choices: Nothing; they may remove them immediately with any force
Ask them to leave, then use no more force than reasonably necessary
Get a court order first, always
Call the land title office
questions.explain: Self-help is allowed only after asking the trespasser to leave, and only with reasonable force.

questions.q: In Segal v. Derrick Golf & Winter Club, golf balls repeatedly landed in a family's backyard. On what basis did the family succeed against the club?
choices: Trespass
Private nuisance
Occupiers' liability
Breach of a restrictive covenant
questions.explain: The club wasn't liable in trespass (its members hit the balls), but it was liable in nuisance for failing to take reasonable steps to stop a serious interference. The family got damages and an injunction.

questions.q: A visitor trips on a loose stair at an open house you're hosting. Under the Occupiers Liability Act, could you be an occupier?
choices: No; only the registered owner is an occupier
Yes; there can be more than one occupier, and a licensee hosting an open house can be one
Only if you own shares in the brokerage
Only if the visitor paid to enter
questions.explain: An occupier is anyone in possession or with responsibility for and control over the premises. There can be several, including a licensee running an open house.
